question: According to the Indiana CDL manual, how far can the danger zone extend from the front bumper of a school bus?
choice_a: 50 feet
choice_b: 20 feet
choice_c: 10 feet
choice_d: 30 feet, with the first 10 feet being the most dangerous
explanation: The danger zone may extend as much as 30 feet from the front bumper of the bus, with the first 10 feet being the most dangerous area.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.1.1 Danger Zones

question: Besides the front, sides, and rear of the bus, what area is always considered dangerous because of passing cars?
choice_a: The area to the left of the bus
choice_b: The area behind the rear axle only
choice_c: The area directly under the bus only
choice_d: The roof of the bus
explanation: The area to the left of the bus is always considered dangerous because of passing cars.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.1.1 Danger Zones

question: When should a school bus driver check that all mirrors are properly adjusted?
choice_a: Only when a student reports a problem
choice_b: Once per week
choice_c: Before operating the school bus, to obtain maximum viewing area
choice_d: Only after the first loading stop
explanation: You should always check each mirror before operating the school bus to obtain maximum viewing area, and have the mirrors adjusted if necessary.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.1.2 Correct Mirror Adjustment

question: When properly adjusted, the outside left and right side flat mirrors should allow the driver to see how far behind the bus?
choice_a: 400 feet
choice_b: 100 feet or 2 bus lengths
choice_c: 200 feet or 4 bus lengths
choice_d: 50 feet
explanation: The outside flat mirrors should be adjusted so the driver can see 200 feet or 4 bus lengths behind the bus, along the sides, and the rear tires touching the ground.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.1.3 Outside Left and Right Side Flat Mirrors

question: The blind spot directly behind a school bus can extend up to what distance, depending on the bus's length and width?
choice_a: 100 feet
choice_b: 400 feet
choice_c: 200 feet
choice_d: 300 feet
explanation: The blind spot behind the bus extends 50 to 150 feet and could extend up to 400 feet depending on the length and width of the bus.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.1.3 Outside Left and Right Side Flat Mirrors

question: What is a key limitation of the outside left and right side convex mirrors?
choice_a: They only function at night
choice_b: They are only used while backing
choice_c: They present a view of people and objects that does not accurately reflect their size and distance from the bus
choice_d: They cannot be adjusted
explanation: Convex mirrors provide a wide-angle view of traffic, clearances, and students at the side of the bus, but they present a view of people and objects that does not accurately reflect their size and distance from the bus.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.1.4 Outside Left and Right Side Convex Mirrors

question: What danger zone area do the outside left and right side crossover mirrors help the driver see that is not visible by direct vision?
choice_a: The roof of the bus
choice_b: The area directly behind the bus
choice_c: The interior aisle of the bus
choice_d: The front bumper danger zone directly in front of the bus
explanation: Crossover mirrors are used to see the front bumper danger zone directly in front of the bus that is not visible by direct vision, as well as the danger zone to the left and right sides including the service door and front wheel area.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.1.5 Outside Left and Right Side Crossover Mirrors

question: What is the primary purpose of the overhead inside rearview mirror on a school bus?
choice_a: To monitor passenger activity inside the bus
choice_b: To check tire clearance
choice_c: To view the railroad crossing
choice_d: To monitor traffic behind the bus
explanation: The overhead inside rearview mirror, mounted above the windshield on the driver's side, is used to monitor passenger activity inside the bus.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.1.6 Overhead Inside Rearview Mirror

question: Can a school bus driver change the location of an official school bus stop on their own judgment?
choice_a: Yes, if the driver notifies dispatch verbally
choice_b: Yes, anytime traffic conditions warrant it
choice_c: No, never without written approval from the appropriate school district official
choice_d: Yes, but only during bad weather
explanation: You should never change the location of a bus stop without written approval from the appropriate school district official.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.2.1 Approaching the Stop

question: If equipped, when should a school bus driver activate the alternating flashing amber warning lights before a stop?
choice_a: Only after coming to a complete stop
choice_b: At least 500 feet before the stop
choice_c: At least 50 feet or 1-2 seconds before the stop
choice_d: At least 200 feet or approximately 5-10 seconds before the stop
explanation: If so equipped, activate alternating flashing amber warning lights at least 200 feet or approximately 5-10 seconds before the school bus stop, or in accordance with state law.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.2.1 Approaching the Stop

question: About how far or how many seconds before pulling over should a driver turn on the right turn signal indicator?
choice_a: 10-20 feet or 1 second
choice_b: 100-300 feet or approximately 3-5 seconds
choice_c: 500 feet or 15 seconds
choice_d: There is no recommended distance
explanation: Turn on the right turn signal indicator about 100-300 feet or approximately 3-5 seconds before pulling over.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.2.1 Approaching the Stop

question: When stopping to load students, how far away from the students at the designated stop should the front bumper come to a stop?
choice_a: At least 20 feet
choice_b: At least 5 feet
choice_c: At least 10 feet
choice_d: Right next to the students
explanation: Bring the school bus to a full stop with the front bumper at least 10 feet away from students at the designated stop, forcing the students to walk to the bus so the driver has a better view of their movements.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.2.1 Approaching the Stop

question: What should a driver do with the transmission and parking brake at each stop?
choice_a: Place the transmission in Park (or Neutral if there is no Park shift point) and set the parking brake
choice_b: Turn off the engine only
choice_c: Leave the transmission in Drive with the brake off
choice_d: Nothing is required
explanation: Place the transmission in Park, or if there is no Park shift point, in Neutral, and set the parking brake at each stop.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.2.1 Approaching the Stop

question: According to the manual, when should students board the school bus?
choice_a: Only when signaled by the driver
choice_b: Only after the dome light is off
choice_c: Whenever they choose
choice_d: As soon as the bus arrives, regardless of signal
explanation: Students should board the bus only when signaled by the driver.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.2.2 Loading Procedures

question: What should the driver do if a student cannot be accounted for at a loading stop?
choice_a: Leave immediately and report it later
choice_b: Radio dispatch and continue the route without stopping
choice_c: Secure the bus, take the key, and check around and underneath the bus
choice_d: Honk the horn repeatedly and depart
explanation: If you cannot account for a student outside, secure the bus, take the key, and check around and underneath the bus.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.2.2 Loading Procedures

question: After exiting the bus along the route, how far should students walk away from the side of the bus to a position where the driver can plainly see them?
choice_a: At least 25 feet
choice_b: At least 5 feet
choice_c: At least 50 feet
choice_d: At least 10 feet
explanation: Tell students to exit the bus and walk at least 10 feet away from the side of the bus to a position where the driver can plainly see all students.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.2.3 Unloading Procedures on the Route

question: Why should the driver count the number of students while unloading?
choice_a: To report attendance to the school office
choice_b: It is not necessary if the route is short
choice_c: To determine fuel usage
choice_d: To confirm the location of all students before pulling away from the stop
explanation: Count the number of students while unloading to confirm the location of all students before pulling away from the stop.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.2.3 Unloading Procedures on the Route

question: When students must cross the roadway after exiting the bus, to what position should they walk before waiting for the driver's signal?
choice_a: Immediately alongside the front bumper
choice_b: At least 10 feet away from the side of the bus, to a point at least 10 feet in front of the right corner of the bumper, remaining away from the front of the bus
choice_c: Across the road without stopping
choice_d: Directly behind the bus
explanation: Students should walk approximately 10 feet away from the side of the bus to a position where the driver can see them, then to a location at least 10 feet in front of the right corner of the bumper while remaining away from the front of the bus.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.2.3 Additional Procedures for Students That Must Cross the Roadway

topic: Special Dangers of Loading and Unloading
question: What should students be told to do if they drop an object near the bus during loading or unloading?
choice_a: Ask another student to retrieve it
choice_b: Ignore it and board through a different door
choice_c: Immediately pick it up and hurry back
choice_d: Leave the object, move to a point of safety out of the danger zones, and try to get the driver's attention
explanation: Students should be told to leave any dropped object and move to a point of safety out of the danger zones and attempt to get the driver's attention to retrieve the object.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.2.5 Special Dangers of Loading and Unloading

topic: Special Dangers of Loading and Unloading
question: What safety hazard is described as a "handrail hang-up"?
choice_a: Students holding hands while boarding
choice_b: A malfunctioning stop signal arm
choice_c: Clothing, accessories, or a body part getting caught in the handrail or door as a student exits
choice_d: Students falling asleep on the bus
explanation: Students have been injured or killed when clothing, accessories, or even parts of their body get caught in the handrail or door as they exited the bus.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.2.5 Special Dangers of Loading and Unloading

question: When conducting a post-trip inspection of a school bus, what should the driver specifically check in addition to articles left on the bus and sleeping students?
choice_a: Mechanical/operational problems, with special attention to mirror systems, flashing warning lamps, and stop signal arms
choice_b: Only the fuel gauge
choice_c: Nothing further is required
choice_d: The bus's paint condition only
explanation: The post-trip inspection should include walking through and around the bus looking for articles left, sleeping students, open windows and doors, and mechanical/operational problems with special attention to items unique to school buses, such as mirror systems, flashing warning lamps, and stop signal arms.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.2.6 Post-trip Inspection

question: As a general rule, when is it safest to keep students on the bus during an emergency?
choice_a: Never; always evacuate immediately
choice_b: When keeping them on the bus does not expose them to unnecessary risk or injury
choice_c: Always, regardless of the situation
choice_d: Only if the bus is still moving
explanation: As a general rule, student safety and control is best maintained by keeping students on the bus during an emergency, if doing so does not expose them to unnecessary risk or injury.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.3.1 Planning for Emergencies

question: Under which of the following conditions must a school bus driver evacuate the bus?
choice_a: The bus is five minutes behind schedule
choice_b: A student requests to change seats
choice_c: The radio is not working
choice_d: The bus is on fire or there is a threat of fire
explanation: The driver must evacuate the bus when it is on fire or there is a threat of fire, among other listed mandatory conditions.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.3.1 Planning for Emergencies -- Mandatory Evacuations

question: Besides fire, which of these is listed as a condition requiring mandatory evacuation of a school bus?
choice_a: The bus is stalled on or adjacent to a railroad-highway crossing
choice_b: The air conditioning has stopped working
choice_c: A student feels carsick
choice_d: The bus is running 10 minutes late
explanation: Mandatory evacuation conditions include the bus being on fire, stalled on or adjacent to a railroad-highway crossing, in a position that may increase danger, in imminent danger of collision, or facing a hazardous materials spill.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.3.1 Planning for Emergencies -- Mandatory Evacuations

question: According to the manual, a "safe place" for evacuated students should be at least how far off the road, in the direction of oncoming traffic?
choice_a: 50 feet
choice_b: 100 feet
choice_c: 200 feet
choice_d: 25 feet
explanation: A safe place will be at least 100 feet off the road in the direction of oncoming traffic, to keep students from being hit by debris if another vehicle collides with the bus.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.3.2 Evacuation Procedures

question: If there is a risk from spilled hazardous materials, how far upwind of the bus should the driver lead students?
choice_a: At least 200 feet
choice_b: At least 50 feet
choice_c: At least 300 feet
choice_d: At least 100 feet
explanation: Lead students upwind of the bus at least 300 feet if there is a risk from spilled hazardous materials.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.3.2 Evacuation Procedures

question: If the bus is in the direct path of a sighted tornado and evacuation is ordered, what should the driver direct students to do if no building shelter is readily available?
choice_a: Escort them to a nearby ditch or culvert and direct them to lie face down with hands covering their heads
choice_b: Send them running in different directions
choice_c: Remain seated with seatbelts fastened
choice_d: Have them stand in a tight group outside the bus
explanation: If the bus is in the direct path of a sighted tornado, escort students to a nearby ditch or culvert if shelter in a building is not readily available, and direct them to lie face down with hands covering their heads, far enough away that the bus cannot topple on them.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.3.2 Evacuation Procedures

question: Before ordering an evacuation, how should the driver secure the bus?
choice_a: Place the transmission in Park (or Neutral), set the parking brakes, shut off the engine, remove the ignition key, and activate hazard-warning lights
choice_b: Leave the engine running for air conditioning
choice_c: No securing steps are needed if the emergency is urgent
choice_d: Only turn off the headlights
explanation: General evacuation procedures include securing the bus by placing the transmission in Park or Neutral, setting parking brakes, shutting off the engine, removing the ignition key, and activating hazard-warning lights.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.3.2 Evacuation Procedures

question: What distinguishes a "passive" railroad-highway crossing from an "active" crossing?
choice_a: Passive crossings are only found in cities
choice_b: A passive crossing has no traffic control device, while an active crossing has a device such as flashing lights or gates
choice_c: There is no difference
choice_d: A passive crossing has gates; an active crossing does not
explanation: Passive crossings do not have any type of traffic control device, and the decision to proceed rests entirely with the driver. Active crossings have a traffic control device such as flashing red lights, with or without bells and gates.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.4.1 Types of Crossings

question: What does the round, black-on-yellow advance warning sign placed ahead of a railroad-highway crossing tell the driver to do?
choice_a: Slow down, look and listen for the train, and be prepared to stop at the tracks
choice_b: Ignore the crossing if no train is visible
choice_c: Change lanes immediately
choice_d: Speed up to clear the crossing quickly
explanation: The advance warning sign tells the driver to slow down, look and listen for the train, and be prepared to stop at the tracks if a train is coming.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.4.2 Warning Signs and Devices

question: At a cross-buck sign, which requires yielding the right-of-way to the train, when must the driver stop before the sign?
choice_a: Only stop if a train is visible
choice_b: Stop before the cross-buck sign if there is no white line painted on the pavement
choice_c: Proceed without stopping if no train is heard
choice_d: Only slow to 20 mph
explanation: The cross-buck sign requires you to yield the right-of-way to the train; if there is no white line painted on the pavement, you must stop the bus before the cross-buck sign.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.4.2 Warning Signs and Devices

question: At a crossing equipped with gates, when should the driver stop?
choice_a: Only if a train whistle is heard
choice_b: When the lights begin to flash and before the gate lowers across the road lane
choice_c: Only after the gate has fully lowered
choice_d: Stopping is not required if gates are present
explanation: Stop when the lights begin to flash and before the gate lowers across the road lane, and remain stopped until the gates go up and the lights have stopped flashing.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.4.2 Warning Signs and Devices -- Gates

question: If the gate remains down after a train has passed, what should the driver do?
choice_a: Back the bus away from the crossing
choice_b: Drive around the gate carefully
choice_c: Not drive around the gate; instead call the dispatcher
choice_d: Wait a reasonable time, then drive through the gate
explanation: If the gate stays down after the train passes, do not drive around the gate; instead, call your dispatcher.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.4.2 Warning Signs and Devices -- Gates

question: When stopping at a railroad-highway crossing, where should the school bus stop in relation to the nearest rail?
choice_a: As close as possible to improve visibility
choice_b: Exactly 25 feet
choice_c: No closer than 5 feet and no farther than 15 feet
choice_d: No closer than 15 feet and no farther than 50 feet
explanation: At the crossing, stop no closer than 15 feet and no farther than 50 feet from the nearest rail, where you have the best view of the tracks.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.4.3 Recommended Procedures -- At the Crossing

question: Approximately how far before a railroad-highway crossing should a driver activate hazard lights to make their intentions known to other traffic?
choice_a: 200 feet
choice_b: 500 feet
choice_c: 100 feet
choice_d: 50 feet
explanation: Activate hazard lights approximately 200 feet before the crossing to make sure your intentions are known.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.4.3 Recommended Procedures -- Approaching the Crossing

question: When approaching a crossing where the far side may not have enough room, what general rule helps a driver determine an acceptable containment or storage area to fully clear the tracks?
choice_a: Add 15 feet to the length of the bus
choice_b: Add 5 feet to the length of the bus
choice_c: Subtract 15 feet from the length of the bus
choice_d: Containment area does not need to be considered
explanation: As a general rule, add 15 feet to the length of the school bus to determine an acceptable amount of containment or storage area on the far side of the crossing.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.4.4 Special Situations -- Containment or Storage Areas

question: If a school bus stalls or becomes trapped on the tracks, what should the driver do?
choice_a: Try to restart the engine before doing anything else
choice_b: Move students to the rear of the bus
choice_c: Get everyone out and off the tracks immediately, moving away at an angle that is both away from the tracks and toward the train
choice_d: Wait inside the bus for help to arrive
explanation: If your bus stalls or is trapped on the tracks, get everyone out and off the tracks immediately. Move everyone far from the bus at an angle that is both away from the tracks and toward the train.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.4.4 Special Situations -- Bus Stalls or Trapped on Tracks

question: At a multiple-track crossing, where should the driver stop, and when should the bus proceed across all of the tracks?
choice_a: Stop before each track individually and check between each one
choice_b: Stop only before the first set of tracks, and proceed across all tracks only when certain no train is approaching on any track
choice_c: Stopping is not required if only one train is visible
choice_d: Proceed as soon as the first train has passed, regardless of the other tracks
explanation: At a multiple-track crossing, stop only before the first set of tracks. When you are sure no train is approaching on any track, proceed across all of the tracks until you have completely cleared them.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.4.3 Recommended Procedures -- Crossing the Track

question: According to the manual, why shouldn't a driver deal with on-bus behavior problems while loading and unloading students?
choice_a: Because behavior problems only occur while the bus is moving
choice_b: Because loading and unloading requires all the driver's concentration
choice_c: Because it is against school policy to discipline students
choice_d: Because students are not allowed to speak during loading
explanation: Loading and unloading requires all of the driver's concentration; the driver should not take their eyes off what is happening outside the bus, so on-bus behavior problems should wait until students are safely off and away.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.5.1 Don't Deal with On-bus Problems When Loading and Unloading

question: When can a school bus driver put a student off the bus for a serious discipline problem?
choice_a: At any safe pull-off location the driver chooses
choice_b: Never, except at school or at the student's designated school bus stop
choice_c: Anywhere along the route as soon as behavior becomes disruptive
choice_d: Only at the next intersection
explanation: Never put a student off the bus except at school or at his or her designated school bus stop. If the offense is serious enough that the driver cannot safely drive the bus, call for a school administrator or the police.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.5.2 Handling Serious Problems

question: Which vehicles does the Department of Transportation require to have antilock braking systems (ABS), according to the manual?
choice_a: Air brake vehicles (trucks, buses, trailers, and converter dollies) built on or after March 1, 1998, and hydraulically braked trucks/buses with a GVWR of 10,000 lbs or more built on or after March 1, 1999
choice_b: Air brake vehicles built before 1990 only
choice_c: All vehicles regardless of brake type or build date
choice_d: Only buses manufactured after 2010
explanation: The Department of Transportation requires ABS on air brake vehicles built on or after March 1, 1998, and on hydraulically braked trucks and buses with a GVWR of 10,000 lbs or more built on or after March 1, 1999.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.6.1 Vehicles Required to Have Antilock Braking Systems

question: How does ABS help a driver on slippery surfaces?
choice_a: It helps avoid wheel lock-up and maintain control, allowing the driver to steer around an obstacle while braking
choice_b: It disables the brakes to prevent skidding
choice_c: It shortens stopping distance in all situations
choice_d: It automatically applies the parking brake
explanation: ABS helps you avoid wheel lock-up and maintain control. You may or may not stop faster with ABS, but you should be able to steer around an obstacle while braking and avoid skids caused by over braking.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.6.2 How ABS Helps You

question: When braking a bus equipped with ABS in an emergency, what should the driver avoid doing?
choice_a: Steering while braking
choice_b: Pumping the brakes
choice_c: Releasing the brakes gradually
choice_d: Applying steady pressure
explanation: Brake the same way regardless of whether the bus has ABS; however, in emergency braking, do not pump the brakes on a bus with ABS.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.6.3 Braking with ABS

question: What does it mean if the yellow ABS malfunction lamp stays on after the start-up bulb check, or comes on while driving?
choice_a: The bus has no brakes at all
choice_b: The bus is out of fuel
choice_c: The driver may have lost ABS control at one or more wheels, though regular brakes still function
choice_d: The parking brake is engaged
explanation: If the lamp stays on after the bulb check, or goes on once underway, you may have lost ABS control at one or more wheels. If ABS malfunctions, you still have regular brakes and should drive normally but get the system serviced soon.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.6.4 Braking if ABS is Not Working

question: Which of the following is true about ABS, according to the manual's safety reminders?
choice_a: ABS compensates for poorly maintained brakes
choice_b: ABS will not necessarily shorten stopping distance, but it helps maintain vehicle control
choice_c: ABS allows the driver to follow other vehicles more closely
choice_d: ABS increases the vehicle's ultimate stopping power
explanation: ABS won't necessarily shorten stopping distance -- it will help maintain vehicle control, but not always shorten stopping distance. ABS also won't allow faster or closer following, won't increase stopping power, and won't compensate for bad brakes.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.6.5 Safety Reminders

question: When should a school bus's roof-mounted white strobe light, if equipped, be used?
choice_a: Only when transporting fewer than 10 students
choice_b: When the driver has limited visibility
choice_c: At all times while the bus is in motion
choice_d: Only during railroad crossings
explanation: If a bus is equipped with a roof-mounted white strobe light, it should be used when the driver has limited visibility, meaning it is difficult to easily see around the bus.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.7.1 Strobe Lights

question: Why do strong winds pose a particular danger to school buses?
choice_a: Winds have no significant effect on buses due to their weight
choice_b: Wind primarily affects the brakes
choice_c: Wind only affects fuel economy
choice_d: The side of the bus acts like a sail on a sailboat and can push the bus sideways or even tip it over
explanation: Strong winds affect the handling of the school bus; the side of a school bus acts like a sail on a sailboat and can push the bus sideways, move it off the road, or, in extreme conditions, tip it over.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.7.2 Driving in High Winds

question: When should a school bus driver back the bus?
choice_a: Backing is never permitted under any circumstance
choice_b: Whenever it saves time on the route
choice_c: Only at night
choice_d: Only when there is no other safe way to move the vehicle, and never with students outside the bus
explanation: Backing a school bus is strongly discouraged. You should back your bus only when you have no other safe way to move the vehicle, and you should never back a school bus when students are outside of the bus.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.7.3 Backing

question: About how much tail swing can a school bus have, requiring the driver to check mirrors during turning movements?
choice_a: Up to ten feet
choice_b: Up to three feet
choice_c: Up to one foot
choice_d: Up to six feet
explanation: A school bus can have up to a three-foot tail swing, so the driver needs to check mirrors before and during any turning movements to monitor it.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 10, 10.7.4 Tail Swing
